title: The numbers at line ends
hookLine: track changes shows every word slipped in; the Granth's numbers do something like it
tomorrow: a ballad, a stair, a couplet: what kinds of poem are in there?

lines: A STROKE, A NUMBER: ONE, TWO.
cards: A shared document with track changes on: every word anyone adds shows up in color, every cut leaves a line through it. Nobody slips anything in quietly. Now look at the end of any verse in the Granth.
A double upright stroke, and a number: one. The next verse, two. At the end of a hymn, two or three numbers can sit side by side.
So, why all the numbers? Part of the answer is a map. Part of it is older than any document app.

teach.b: First, the map. Each verse closes with its number. At a hymn's end you may see the last verse's number, then the hymn's own number in its group, and in places a running count.
The rahao carries a number too. So the numbers guide: where a verse stops, where the center is, where one hymn ends and the next begins. Second, the guard.
When every verse and hymn is counted, a line slipped in or dropped out would show. Guru Amar Das, in the Anand, says in paraphrase that apart from the True Guru's, every other word is unripe.
The Granth keeps its words, and the numbers help keep them. Now a neighbor, in its own words. Jewish tradition carries this same care.
In Deuteronomy, in the 1917 JPS translation: "Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you."
Shared ground: sacred words kept whole, nothing added, nothing taken away. And one honest difference.
In Deuteronomy, Moses is speaking about God's commandments, words to be lived as law.
In the Granth, the words being kept are the Gurus' hymns, sung, and honored by Sikhs as the Guru itself, with the counting built into the page.
Something to tell a friend tonight: two traditions, in their own words, guard their scripture from even one extra line.

how: In the Guru Granth Sahib each verse ends with a number between double strokes, and each hymn closes with its own numbers; readers use them to find their place, and the fixed text is copied and printed without additions.

games.q: a classmate flips through your gutka and says the numbers are just a printing trick, nothing to do with faith. what's the fair reply?
o: they guide readers, and they guard the words, so a line added or lost would show.
she's right: the numbers are only there for convenience, with no meaning at all.
they tell the reader how many times to repeat each verse before moving on.
games.why: the numbers are a map and a guard. Guru Amar Das calls every word but the True Guru's unripe; Deuteronomy says ye shall not add. different words, shared care.

practice: Open any hymn and count its verses on your fingers, one finger for each number at a line's end. When you reach the last one, look at the numbers sitting side by side.
Then breathe slowly, one breath for each verse you counted, and let the count carry you to the end of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The numbers at line ends: the numbers that close each verse and each hymn in the Granth, counting them like an index built into the page. The eighth word of the year.

orig.note: Gurmukhi numerals one to four, the kind of numbers that close each verse.

carryVoice: Something to keep: the numbers guide, and they guard what they count. Eight of twenty, counted.
